sentences.text: Thirty sailors ran across a brand-new warship until she nearly rolled over, and the navy sent her to sea anyway.
The admiral stops the test and mutters, "If only the king were here."
But the king is off at war, and he wants the mightiest warship afloat.
So the Vasa gets two decks of heavy bronze cannons, stacked high above the water.
Nobody wants to tell the king his masterpiece wobbles.
His letters keep arriving: "Get her to sea."
On launch day, a huge crowd watches her sails go up.
One light gust leans her over.
She shakes it off, and the crowd keeps waving.
Then a second gust tips her further, and her open lower gun ports dip under the water.
The sea pours in, and in front of the whole city, the Vasa sinks inside her own harbour.
At the hearing, one builder's best explanation is, "Only God knows."
The man who ordered the cannons was the king.
You see, a ship stays upright like a bottle with sand in the bottom: heavy low, light on top.
The Vasa was built upside down, with tons of bronze up high and too little stone below.
And more stone would only have pushed those gun ports down to the waterline.
So when thirty sailors nearly rolled her over at the dock, the Vasa was showing them exactly how she would sink.
